title: Cover any 3D convex body with 13 smaller copies
premise_risks: a 2026 preprint lowering 14 could exist outside the search results
plain: Take any bounded convex solid in space. How many strictly smaller copies of it (scaled down, translated, not rotated) are always enough to cover it? A cube needs 8, and Hadwiger conjectured 8 always suffice. The best proved number is 14. Prove that 13 always suffice.
math: For a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ let $H(K)$ be the least $m$ such that $K\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^m (\lambda K + t_i)$ for some $0<\lambda<1$, $t_i\in\mathbb R^3$ (equivalently the illumination number). Let $H_3=\sup_K H(K)$. Known $8\le H_3\le 14$. Prove $H_3\le 13$.
review_note: Known: $H_3\le14$: A. Prymak, 'A new bound for Hadwiger's covering problem in $\mathbb E^3$', SIAM J. Discrete Math. 37 (2023) 17–24, arXiv:2112.10698. Earlier $H_3\le16$: Papadoperakis, Geom. Dedicata 75 (1999); $H_3\le20$: Lassak (1984). Lower bound 8 (cube). Centrally symmetric case $=8$ (Lassak). Cap bodies in $\mathbb R^3$ have illumination number 6 (arXiv:2507.08712, 2025). Arman–Bondarenko–Prymak, Canad. Math. Bull. 68 (2025), arXiv:2404.00547: small dimensions $\ge5$, no change for $n=3$.
